plants.name: Holly
plants.guide: The hollies on the property are tough and well-suited to these slopes — full sun for the best berry production, partial shade tolerated. Acidic well-drained soil. Most species need both male and female plants for berries. Established hollies are quite drought-tolerant. Watch for leaf miner and scale insects.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Early May — new growth flush starting at Church Mountain Road. Hold off on heavy pruning until that flush hardens off in early summer — pruning now would remove flower buds.
plants.soilNotes: Well-matched to Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils (pH 4.5–6.0). Most hollies thrive in the 5.5–6.5 range — you may need light dolomitic lime applications on more acidic spots at Church Mountain Road. Both Ilex opaca (American holly, native) and Ilex cornuta (Chinese holly) perform excellently here. Established plants tolerate clay subsoil reasonably well — better drainage tolerance than most landscape shrubs.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun for maximum berry production. East-facing slopes at Church Mountain Road are excellent — good sun exposure without the desiccating northwest winter winds that affect exposed ridgeline positions. Berry-bearing female plants need a male holly within about 50 feet (within pollinator range) — plan your male/female planting accordingly.
plants.frostSensitivity: Very hardy — most Ilex species are Zone 5 or colder. Flowers (and therefore berries) can be lost to a late frost in late April; at Church Mountain Road elevation (~2,959 ft), the bloom window (late April–May) slightly overlaps the last frost probability window. Mature berries persist through winter and easily tolerate Zone 7b low temperatures.

subcategories.label: Shaping
subcategories.peakWindow: Jun 23–Jul 13 at ~2,959 ft — after spring flush hardened, before late-summer bud set
subcategories.description: Early-to-mid summer (Jun–Jul) after the spring growth flush has hardened. At Church Mountain Road elevation, this window lands about a week later than valley plants — typically late June through early July. Pruning earlier removes flowers (= no berries this year). Pruning later interferes with bud set for next year's berries. For berry-producing female plants, prune lightly to preserve flowering branches.

subcategories.label: Hard renovation
subcategories.peakWindow: Feb 18–Mar 8
subcategories.description: Late winter (Feb–early Mar) for severely overgrown hollies that need to be cut hard. Hollies tolerate hard pruning well, even down to bare wood — they regenerate from old wood, which is unusual among broadleaf evergreens. Sacrifices berries for one season but restores shape. Use only when needed; not part of normal annual care.

propagate.description: Semi-hardwood cuttings in mid-to-late summer (Jul–Sep). 4-6 inch cuttings, hormone, well-drained mix. Rooting takes 8–12 weeks. Hollies are dioecious — you'll need both male and female plants for berries, so propagate accordingly. Seed propagation is slow (often 2-year germination) and seedlings have unknown sex until flowering.

fertilize.description: Two feedings: early spring (Mar) before bud break, and again after flowering (May at elevation) to support berry development. Use an acidic fertilizer formulated for evergreens. Yellow leaves often indicate iron chlorosis from soil pH that's drifted too alkaline — soil test before assuming nutrient deficiency.

water.description: Established hollies are quite drought-tolerant, but young plants and any holly trying to set a heavy berry crop need consistent water Jun–Sep. Deep weekly watering during dry stretches.

repot.description: Not applicable for landscape hollies.

subcategories.label: Leaf miner
subcategories.peakWindow: May 4–20
subcategories.description: May: squiggly trails or blotches inside leaves. Mostly cosmetic on established hollies. Prune off heavily affected leaves and destroy them; treat with systemic if severe.

subcategories.label: Scale insects
subcategories.description: Jun–Jul: small bumpy growths on stems and leaf undersides; sticky honeydew below the plant; black sooty mold on lower leaves. Treat with horticultural oil during dormancy or systemic insecticide during the active growing season.

subcategories.label: Spider mites
subcategories.description: Aug–Sep hot dry stretches: bronze stippling, fine webbing on leaf undersides. Hose off forcefully or treat with miticide if severe.

plants.name: Mountain Laurel
plants.guide: The mountain laurels here are Blue Ridge natives — the property's woodland edges sit squarely in their habitat. Wants acidic well-drained soil, partial shade, and good air circulation. Avoid wet feet at all costs. Slow-growing and long-lived. Deadhead spent blooms to channel energy into next year's flowering. All parts are toxic to livestock and pets.
plants.currentSeasonNote: In May at Church Mountain — flower buds swelling for May–June bloom at Church Mountain Road elevation. Don't prune now — wait until just after flowering finishes. This is one of the most spectacular spring plants on the property.
plants.soilNotes: Native Blue Ridge species — Church Mountain Road is in its core Appalachian habitat and the Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils are its native medium. Thrives at pH 4.5–5.5 without any amendment. The native leaf litter of the property's wooded areas is the ideal mulch. Critical weakness: waterlogged roots — the well-drained slopes of Church Mountain Road are ideal, but any flat spot with clay Bt subsoil is high-risk. Test drainage in suspect areas before planting.
plants.aspectPreference: North-facing and east-facing mid-slope woodland edges are perfect at Church Mountain Road — exactly where mountain laurel occurs naturally. South-facing direct-sun exposures are too hot and dry for it even at elevation. The property's native woodland with dappled canopy is prime mountain laurel habitat; the plants already established there are in their optimal zone.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4. Very cold-tolerant at Church Mountain Road elevation. Flower buds are frost-sensitive in spring — a late freeze after bud swell in late April or early May can kill developing flowers without harming the plant. At ~2,959 ft, the May 1–15 window is the critical frost-risk period for buds. Established plants at this elevation are fully winter-hardy.

prune.peakWindow: Jun 18–Jul 8 at ~2,959 ft — immediately after last flowers drop
prune.description: Single window: immediately after flowering ends. At Church Mountain Road elevation, blooms peak in late May–early June, about a week later than valley plants — the pruning window opens in mid-June and closes by early July. Like azaleas, mountain laurel sets next year's buds on summer growth, so pruning later removes next year's flowers. Deadheading spent blooms is the most useful task — it prevents seed formation and channels energy into bud set. Heavy renovation should be done in stages over 2–3 years; mountain laurel is slow to recover from hard cuts.

subcategories.label: Layering
subcategories.description: Best home propagation method but slow — 1–2 years for usable roots. Bend a low branch to the ground, wound the underside, dust with rooting hormone, pin and cover with soil. Patience required. Spring or fall are both good start times.

subcategories.label: Cuttings (low success)
subcategories.peakWindow: Jul 13–Aug 2
subcategories.description: Jul–Aug semi-hardwood cuttings. Honestly difficult — under 20% success even with bottom heat and mist. Most home gardeners give up after one attempt. If you want more mountain laurel, buy nursery stock or do layering.

fertilize.description: Light hand. Early spring (Mar) and after flowering (late June at elevation) with an acidic fertilizer. Mountain laurel evolved on lean rocky mountain soils — Church Mountain Road's native soil actually mimics its natural conditions. Over-fertilizing causes more harm than under-fertilizing. If your plant is established in good acidic soil with leaf litter mulch, it may need no supplemental feeding at all.

water.description: Surprisingly drought-tolerant once established, but they hate wet feet. Apr–Jul is the most critical window — they're flowering and setting next year's buds. Deep occasional watering beats frequent shallow watering. Avoid overhead watering — wet foliage promotes leaf spot diseases. Church Mountain Road's orographic rainfall (estimated 60–65 in/yr) means established plants rarely need irrigation except in drought years.

repot.description: Not applicable.

subcategories.label: Leaf spot
subcategories.description: Apr–Jun in cool wet springs: brown or purple spots on leaves. Usually cosmetic. Improve air circulation, avoid overhead watering, rake fallen leaves. Church Mountain Road's cool spring temperatures and high humidity make this more common than at lower elevations.

subcategories.label: Lace bugs
subcategories.description: Jun–Jul: silvery stippling on upper leaf surfaces, similar to azalea damage. Look for the bugs themselves on undersides. More common on plants in too much sun — another reason to site mountain laurel in shaded woodland positions. Treat with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil.

subcategories.label: Root rot (phytophthora)
subcategories.description: Jul–Aug: any wilting that doesn't recover overnight is typically phytophthora root rot. Often fatal and caused by poor drainage. At Church Mountain Road, any plant placed in a flat area with clay Bt subsoil is at risk. Improve drainage if possible; replace lost plants in better-drained spots — a well-drained mid-slope position at Church Mountain Road will almost never see this disease.

plants.name: Japanese Maple
plants.guide: The Japanese maples on the property want afternoon shade — direct hot summer sun scorches the leaves, especially on the dissectum (laceleaf) varieties. Want well-drained acidic soil rich in organic matter. Shallow roots demand consistent moisture and mulch. Pruning is best in late winter or summer — avoid spring when sap flows heavily.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Looking at the month — leaves fully out at Church Mountain Road. Avoid pruning now — sap flow is at its peak. Mulch thoroughly before summer heat arrives and watch for aphids on new growth. This is the most frost-vulnerable growth stage for Japanese maples at elevation.
plants.soilNotes: Excellent match for Church Mountain Road soils. Hayesville sandy loam surface horizon provides excellent drainage while retaining adequate moisture when amended with compost. Native pH 4.5–5.5 is in the ideal range for Japanese maples (5.0–6.0). Annual leaf mulch at 2–3 inches is the most valuable single amendment — it moderates soil temperature, retains moisture, and feeds beneficial fungi. Avoid clay subsoil flat areas where drainage is poor and root rot risk increases.
plants.aspectPreference: East-facing mid-slope is the ideal Church Mountain Road position. Afternoon shade is essential — the property's east-facing slopes provide natural afternoon shade from the mountain. South-facing slopes at this elevation consistently cause leaf scorch on dissectum types even with irrigation. North-facing positions reduce fall color intensity. The thermal belt mid-slope positions are safest against late spring frosts that can damage the early leaf flush.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 5b. New spring growth is very frost-sensitive — a late freeze after leaf flush (at Church Mountain Road: watch the May 1–21 window) can kill or brown the entire first flush of leaves. Trees recover but lose a season of growth. Dissectum (laceleaf) types push leaves earlier than upright types and are more frost-exposed at elevation. Site away from frost pockets — thermal belt mid-slope positions at Church Mountain Road are significantly safer than any hollow or valley bottom.

subcategories.label: Structural pruning
subcategories.peakWindow: Jan 18–Feb 13 before sap surge — hard cutoff at mid-February
subcategories.description: Late winter (Jan–Feb) while fully dormant — branch architecture is visible and sap flow is minimal. Remove dead, damaged, crossing, and inward-growing branches. Establish the long-term framework. CRITICAL cutoff: stop by mid-February. Pruning in early spring (Mar–Apr) hits peak sap flow; cuts will bleed heavily and may not heal cleanly. At Church Mountain Road elevation bud break occurs slightly later than the valley, giving you a small extended window — but mid-February remains the safe cutoff.

subcategories.label: Summer refinement
subcategories.peakWindow: Jul 18–Aug 7 at ~2,959 ft — sap at seasonal low
subcategories.description: Mid-to-late summer (Jul–Aug) sap flow has slowed. Best window for refinement work — thinning the canopy for light penetration, removing water sprouts, improving silhouette. Cuts heal quickly. You can see the full leaf canopy and shape it precisely. At Church Mountain Road, Jul 18–Aug 7 is ideal. Never prune in fall — wounds invite winter dieback.

propagate.description: Most cultivars (named varieties like 'Bloodgood' or any laceleaf type) are grafted onto seedling rootstock and won't come true from cuttings or seed — propagation is for specialists. Species Acer palmatum can be grown from seed (collect samaras in fall, cold-stratify, sow in spring), but seedlings are highly variable. If you want more of a specific cultivar, it's nursery stock only.

fertilize.description: Early spring (Mar–Apr) with a slow-release acidic fertilizer, light hand. Japanese maples are slow growers and over-fertilizing produces weak floppy growth. Most established trees in Church Mountain Road's naturally acidic organic-matter-rich soil need little or no fertilizer — yellow or pale leaves usually indicate pH issues, not nutrient deficiency. Test soil pH before fertilizing.

water.description: Shallow-rooted and very drought-sensitive. Jun–Sep is critical, especially during hot dry stretches. Afternoon shade is more important than supplemental water — direct hot afternoon sun causes leaf scorch even in well-watered trees, especially for laceleaf varieties. Site these on east-facing slopes at Church Mountain Road where natural afternoon shade is available. Deep mulch and consistent moisture prevent most problems.

repot.description: Container Japanese maples should be repotted every 2–3 years in late winter (Feb), with light root pruning to maintain scale.

subcategories.label: Aphids
subcategories.peakWindow: Apr 18–May 13 at ~2,959 ft — peak aphid flush on new growth
subcategories.description: Apr–May on tender new growth: clusters of green or black insects, sticky honeydew below. At Church Mountain Road elevation, the peak flush of tender new growth occurs about a week later than valley plants. Hose off forcefully; insecticidal soap if heavy. Ladybugs and parasitic wasps handle most infestations naturally — avoid broad-spectrum pesticides that kill beneficial insects.

subcategories.label: Leaf scorch (heat/sun)
subcategories.description: Jun–Aug: browning leaf margins from sun and heat stress, especially in trees with too much afternoon exposure. Worst on laceleaf varieties. Mostly cosmetic — won't kill the tree but indicates a siting problem. Increase mulch, ensure consistent water, consider transplanting to a more shaded east-facing position in fall.

subcategories.label: Verticillium wilt
subcategories.description: Jun–Aug: sudden branch dieback, dark streaks visible in cut wood. Often fatal — soil-borne fungus, no cure. Remove affected branches well below symptoms; sterilize tools. If the whole tree dies, don't replant another Japanese maple in the same spot — the fungus persists in soil for many years.

plants.name: Pyracomeles (Berry Box)
plants.guide: The Berry Box® pyracomeles on the property is a compact intergeneric evergreen — a hybrid of pyracantha and osteomeles bred for fine boxwood-like foliage, white spring flowers, and red berries that hold from fall through winter. Stays naturally tight at 2–3 ft tall and wide with no shearing required. Tolerant of full sun to part shade and most well-drained soils. Drought-tolerant once established. Low maintenance — much of the appeal is that it gives the boxwood look without boxwood blight risk.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Right now — white flower clusters peak now or just finished. Once bloom is over, light shaping is fine. Watch for aphids on new growth — soft spring tips are their favorite landing zone.
plants.soilNotes: Tolerant of Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils as long as drainage is good. Slightly acidic to neutral pH (5.5–7.0) preferred. The clay Bt subsoil at Church Mountain Road is fine for Pyracomeles — it has deeper roots than boxwood and handles transitional drainage. Avoid permanently wet low spots.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun to light shade. South, east, and west exposures all work. North-facing positions reduce flower and berry display by 30–50%. Best berry production on south or east-facing slopes with morning-to-midday sun.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy USDA Zone 6–9. Solidly within range at Church Mountain Road's elevation-adjusted Zone 6b. No winter protection needed for established plants. Late frosts (post-May 10) can damage open flowers but rarely hurt the plant itself.

prune.peakWindow: May 15–June 5 — once spring flowers finish, before berries set
prune.description: Light shaping after flowering. Tip-prune any stray shoots; never shear the way you would a boxwood — Berry Box has a naturally rounded form and shearing creates twiggy interior dead zones. Avoid pruning after July: that removes the developing berries which are the best feature of the plant. If hard renewal is needed (rare), do it in late winter (Feb).

propagate.description: Berry Box is patented (USPP35913) — propagation for sale is prohibited. For personal use, semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer root reasonably well in 50/50 perlite and peat with bottom heat. Most home gardeners simply buy additional plants from the nursery.

fertilize.description: Early spring with a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g. Espoma Plant-tone 5-3-3). Acidic soil amendments not required. Established plants in good soil rarely need more than a single spring feed. Over-fertilizing produces lush growth at the expense of berry display.

water.description: Weekly deep watering for the first two summers after planting (May–Sep). Established plants are drought-tolerant and rarely need supplemental water at Church Mountain Road's 60–65 in/yr rainfall. During extended summer drought, water deeply once every 10–14 days.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape shrub, not a container plant.

subcategories.label: Spring aphids
subcategories.peakWindow: Apr 15–May 20 on new growth
subcategories.description: Look for clusters of small green or black aphids on new shoot tips. Strong jet of water knocks most populations off. Severe infestations: insecticidal soap or neem in early evening. Avoid systemic neonicotinoids — they kill pollinators visiting the flowers.

subcategories.label: Spider mites
subcategories.peakWindow: Jul 10–Aug 20 in dry hot stretches
subcategories.description: Hot dry July–August conditions favor spider mites. Symptoms: stippled yellowish foliage and fine webbing on undersides of leaves. Hose down foliage every few days during hot dry weeks to suppress populations. Severe cases: horticultural oil spray in cool morning.

bloom.window: Small white flowers in spring, then berries
bloom.note: Grown mostly for the berry display that follows.

plants.name: Yuki Cherry Blossom Deutzia
plants.guide: The Yuki Cherry Blossom® deutzia here is a petite spreading shrub bred for compact (12–24 inch) habit and abundant pink spring flowers. Excellent for borders, edges of beds, and ground-cover-style massing. Burgundy fall foliage. Easy to grow in average soils. Deer browse occasionally — usually skipped if other choices are available.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Early May — peak bloom or just finishing at Church Mountain Road's elevation. Wait until bloom completely finishes before any pruning — deutzias bloom on previous-year wood, so summer or fall pruning sacrifices next spring's flowers.
plants.soilNotes: Tolerant of Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils. Prefers slightly acidic (5.5–6.5), moist, well-drained loam. The native pH range at Church Mountain Road is ideal. Mulch 2 inches with shredded hardwood or pine straw to keep roots cool through summer. Heavy clay at the Bt subsoil layer is acceptable as long as the surface drains.
plants.aspectPreference: Best in 4–6 hours of sun (part to full sun). South-east and east-facing slopes are ideal — morning sun with afternoon shade keeps the pink flowers from fading prematurely. Full afternoon sun in west/south positions works but bloom color may pale.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy USDA Zone 5–8 (down to −20°F). Solid for Church Mountain Road. New growth emerging in April–May is frost-sensitive — a hard late-April freeze can blacken the leaf tips. Plant recovers fully; no intervention needed.

prune.description: Critical timing: Yuki Cherry Blossom blooms on previous-year wood. Prune ONLY after flowers have completely finished, before mid-June. Light renewal — remove the oldest 1/3 of stems at the base every 2–3 years to keep the plant vigorous. Any pruning after July removes next spring's flower buds. The plant 'seldom needs pruning' per Proven Winners — it stays naturally compact.

propagate.description: Patented cultivar (Deutzia 'NCDX2') — commercial propagation prohibited. For personal use: softwood cuttings in early summer root readily in moist perlite-peat mix under intermittent mist. Most gardeners simply purchase additional plants for additional plantings.

fertilize.description: Early spring with a balanced slow-release fertilizer (Espoma Plant-tone or similar). Established plants in good soil rarely need more than annual feeding. Skip if growth is already vigorous — over-fertilizing produces lush foliage at the expense of next year's flowers.

water.description: Weekly during the first two summers after planting. Established plants are moderately drought-tolerant but appreciate a deep weekly soak during July–August dry spells. The shallow root system benefits from consistent moisture and 2-inch mulch.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape shrub. Could be grown in large containers but not typical.

inspect.description: Generally pest- and disease-free. Watch new spring growth for occasional aphid clusters; hose off if found. Deer browse occasionally — Proven Winners rates deer resistance as 'low,' meaning deer may sample but typically don't decimate. If deer pressure is heavy, repellent spray in early spring helps establish 'avoid' association.

plants.name: Clematis (large-flowered hybrid)

variety.note: a photo read — the pale-pink kind with a rosy stripe down each petal, vs a deeper rose

plants.guide: The clematis on the east-facing deck trellis climbs by twisting its leaf petioles around any thin support — the cable rail does the job nicely. Pink-and-magenta bicolor flowers with a darker bar down each tepal. Group 2 clematis bloom twice: once in late May–June on previous year's wood, then a smaller second flush in August on new wood. The classic gardener's wisdom: 'cool feet, warm head' — keep the roots shaded and cool with mulch or low plantings, let the vine itself climb into sun.
plants.currentSeasonNote: In May at Church Mountain — vines should be actively growing and approaching bloom. First flowers typically open mid- to late-May at Church Mountain Road's elevation. If buds look swollen, peak bloom is 1–2 weeks out. Now is a fine time to apply mulch and check that the support trellis is firmly anchored before flower weight piles on.
plants.soilNotes: Prefers neutral to slightly alkaline soil (pH 6.5–7.5). Church Mountain Road's native acidic Hayesville soils are below that range — top-dress with a small handful of garden lime around the base each spring (no more than 1 cup per plant). Heavy mulch (3 inches) over the root zone is essential to keep roots cool. Avoid letting bark or organic mulch touch the stem directly — leave a 2-inch gap.
plants.aspectPreference: Vine in full to part sun (6+ hours). Roots in shade. The east-facing deck cable-rail trellis location is excellent — morning sun for blooms, afternoon shade for the soil. Avoid hot south or west positions where roots overheat.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy USDA Zone 4–9. Solid for Church Mountain Road. The vine dies back partially in winter but the woody base survives. Late spring frosts can blacken emerging shoots; the plant pushes new growth from lower nodes within a few weeks.

subcategories.label: Light spring pruning (Group 2)
subcategories.peakWindow: Feb 20–Mar 10 before bud swell
subcategories.description: Group 2 clematis (large-flowered, twice-blooming hybrids like 'Nelly Moser' / 'Dr. Ruppel') need only LIGHT pruning. Late winter, before bud swell: remove dead and weak stems at the base; shorten remaining stems back to the strongest pair of fat green buds. Don't cut hard to the ground — that sacrifices the May–June bloom which comes from old wood.

subcategories.label: Deadhead after first bloom
subcategories.peakWindow: Jun 15–Jul 5 — when first flush finishes
subcategories.description: After the May–June bloom finishes, snip off spent flowers down to the next strong leaf pair. This encourages the August second flush on new wood. Optional but improves the secondary display.

propagate.peakWindow: May 25–Jun 20 — soft layering or stem cuttings
propagate.description: Easy to propagate by ground layering: in late spring, bend a low pliable stem to the soil, nick the underside, pin it down with a u-shaped wire, and cover with 2 inches of soil. By the following spring it will have rooted; sever and transplant. Stem cuttings (2-node sections) in early summer also work in moist perlite under shade.

subcategories.label: Spring feed
subcategories.peakWindow: Mar 15–Apr 5
subcategories.description: Balanced slow-release fertilizer in early spring (e.g. Espoma Tomato-tone or Plant-tone). Top-dress with composted manure or finished compost around the root zone.

subcategories.label: After first bloom
subcategories.peakWindow: Jun 15–Jul 5
subcategories.description: Light second feeding after the May–June bloom finishes — supports the August re-bloom. Liquid feed (kelp, fish emulsion) applied at half strength is gentler than another granular dose.

water.description: Deep weekly water during the growing season. Clematis is shallow-rooted (top 12 inches) and sensitive to drought stress — a wilted vine in mid-summer often loses its second bloom flush. Water at the base; avoid wetting foliage in the evening to reduce powdery mildew risk.

repot.description: Not applicable for in-ground plantings. Container clematis (rare) would refresh top-third of soil annually in early spring.

subcategories.label: Clematis wilt
subcategories.description: Sudden collapse of one or more stems mid-spring is the classic clematis wilt — a fungal infection (Phoma clematidina) that enters at soil level. Cut affected stems all the way to the ground and dispose (don't compost). The crown almost always survives and re-sprouts from below ground. Mature plants outgrow susceptibility; younger plants are most at risk.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: Whitish powder on leaves in humid summer weather. Improve air circulation around the trellis. Avoid overhead watering. Severe cases: a milk-water spray (1:9) or potassium bicarbonate fungicide. Cosmetic, rarely fatal.

bloom.window: Late spring, with a lighter repeat in late summer
bloom.note: Group 2 — the big first flush is on old wood, a second lighter flush on new growth.

plants.name: Hosta (mixed cultivars)
plants.scientificName: Hosta sp. (multiple cultivars in the bed)
plants.guide: The hostas in the stone-walled bed are foliage perennials of the shade garden — multiple cultivars sharing the same care. Dies completely to ground each winter; emerges as tightly furled spear-shaped 'pips' in late April–May at this elevation. Once unfurled, the leaves stay until first frost. Lavender or white late-summer flower scapes. Multiple cultivars in this bed — blue-grey corrugated heart-leaf type (likely H. sieboldiana family), white-margined variegated forms (Patriot/Francee family), and chartreuse types (Sum and Substance family). All share the same care.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Looking at the month — pips have emerged and leaves are unfurling. This is the prime window for slug-baiting BEFORE serious damage starts — by the time leaves are fully open, slugs have already found them. Apply iron-phosphate slug bait (Sluggo or Escar-Go, pet-safe) around the base now.
plants.soilNotes: Prefers moist, fertile, well-drained loam with high organic matter. Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet native soils benefit from annual compost top-dressing. Slightly acidic (5.5–6.5) is ideal. Tolerant of clay if surface drainage is decent. The stone-walled bed location is excellent — the wall provides cool root run and the bed accumulates organic matter from leaf litter.
plants.aspectPreference: Shade to morning sun. East and north-facing positions are ideal at Church Mountain Road. Blue-leaf cultivars retain their waxy bloom best in full shade — direct sun causes them to fade to dusty green. Variegated forms tolerate more sun but burn at edges in afternoon heat. Chartreuse forms color best with 2–4 hours of dappled sun.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy USDA Zone 3–9. Bulletproof for Church Mountain Road. Late frosts AFTER pips emerge can blacken the new leaves — a hard freeze post-May 10 can damage the season's display. If a late frost is forecast, drape with old sheets or upturned buckets overnight; remove in the morning.

prune.peakWindow: Nov 1–20 after first hard frost flattens the foliage
prune.description: Cut back blackened foliage after the first hard frost (typically late October–early November at this elevation). Or wait until early spring before pips emerge (Feb–early March). Composting the spent leaves is fine if no slug eggs are visible underneath. Some gardeners leave the foliage as winter cover for the crowns; either approach works.

propagate.description: Divide every 4–5 years in EARLY spring, before the leaves unfurl — once leaves are open, division causes a season of stress. Lift the entire clump with a fork; separate by hand or with a sharp spade into chunks each carrying 2–3 pips and a section of root. Replant immediately, water in. Narrow window — don't rush past it.

fertilize.description: Light feeding at emergence with a balanced slow-release fertilizer (10-10-10 or Plant-tone). Top-dress with 1 inch of compost around (not on) the crown. Hostas are not heavy feeders — over-fertilizing produces floppy leaves susceptible to wind tear.

water.description: Deep weekly water through the growing season — hostas wilt visibly when dry and recover slowly. Apply 2–3 inches of mulch (shredded hardwood or pine straw) to retain moisture. The stone-walled bed will dry faster than open ground; check more frequently during July–August dry spells.

repot.description: Not applicable for in-ground plantings. Container hostas (sometimes used for accent) would refresh soil and divide every 2–3 years in early spring.

subcategories.label: Slug damage
subcategories.peakWindow: May 1–Jun 30 — emerging leaves are slug magnets
subcategories.description: The single biggest hosta problem at Church Mountain Road's humid climate. Symptoms: irregular holes chewed in the leaves, especially overnight. Bait with iron-phosphate pellets (Sluggo, Escar-Go) at emergence and re-apply after each heavy rain. Beer traps work but need refilling. Avoid thick mulch right against the crown — it shelters slugs.

subcategories.label: Deer browsing
subcategories.description: Hostas are notorious deer candy. At Church Mountain Road, deer pressure is significant. Repellent spray (Liquid Fence or homemade egg-and-garlic) every 2–3 weeks during the growing season is the most reliable defense. Physical fencing or cages around prized cultivars in heavy-pressure years.

plants.name: Pond Iris (Blue Flag)
plants.guide: The native Blue Flag holds the pond edge, its rhizomes anchored in mud and strap-like sword-shaped foliage rising out of the shallows. Deep purple/violet falls and standards with a yellow-and-white signal patch. Spreads gradually by rhizome extension — clumps double in size every 3–5 years. The well-behaved neighbor to the pond's Yellow Flag. Very low maintenance once established; the pond does most of the work.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Right now — bloom's finished for the year (peak here runs mid-May into June). A fine time to thin out any decaying foliage sitting in the water, which adds organic load as it breaks down. Unlike its Yellow Flag pondmate, the native Blue Flag stays put and doesn't need its seed heads chased down.
plants.soilNotes: Lives in pond mud and shallow water (0–4 inches over the rhizome). The pond's accumulated organic sediment provides all nutrition needed. No amendment required. Tolerant of seasonal water-level fluctuation as long as the rhizome stays consistently moist.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun for best bloom. Tolerates light shade but flower count drops 30–50%. The pond location with open sky exposure is ideal. North-bank plantings get more sun (south-facing aspect into the pond); south-bank plantings get less.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy USDA Zone 3–9. Bulletproof. Native species; built for North Georgia winters. Foliage dies back to the rhizome after first hard frost; new shoots emerge in April.

subcategories.label: Remove spent bloom stalks
subcategories.peakWindow: Jun 5–25 after flowering finishes
subcategories.description: Snip spent flower stalks at the base after each bloom. Prevents seed-pod formation, which redirects energy back to the rhizome. Especially important in pond settings where mass seeding can crowd the planting.

subcategories.label: Cut back foliage in late fall
subcategories.peakWindow: After first hard frost flattens leaves
subcategories.description: Cut foliage to about 6 inches above the water surface after frost has killed back the leaves. Removing the dead foliage from the water reduces decomposition load on the pond and limits overwintering iris borer eggs (their preferred winter habitat is in old leaf debris).

propagate.description: Divide rhizomes every 3–5 years to prevent overcrowding. Lift the clump with a fork (or pull from the mud), wash off muck to expose the rhizome network, cut into sections each with a healthy fan of leaves and several inches of root. Replant immediately at the same depth as before — rhizome top barely covered, leaf bases above water. August–early September timing avoids stressing during peak summer heat and gives roots time to re-establish before winter.

fertilize.description: Light feeding only. Pond iris in established ponds rarely need fertilizer — the pond's organic load supplies plenty. If bloom is poor, slow-release aquatic fertilizer tablets (e.g. Pondtabbs) pushed into the mud around the rhizome in early spring help. Excessive fertilizer causes lush leaves at the expense of bloom and can drive pond algae blooms.

water.description: Not applicable — lives in the pond. No supplemental irrigation needed.

repot.description: Not applicable for pond-edge plantings. Container-grown specimens (rare for Blue Flag) would refresh aquatic potting mix every 2–3 years in early spring.

subcategories.label: Iris borer
subcategories.peakWindow: May 10–Jun 15 — larvae feed inside leaf bases
subcategories.description: The most serious iris pest. Adult moths lay eggs on dead foliage in fall; larvae hatch in spring and tunnel down through new leaves into the rhizome where they cause soft rot. Symptoms: water-soaked or 'bleeding' streaks on leaves; ragged chewed leaf edges; foul-smelling rhizomes. Control: remove and destroy ALL old foliage in late fall (eliminates overwintering eggs). If borers found in spring, squash them inside the leaf channel or remove the affected fan entirely. Iron-phosphate slug bait near the base in early spring can disrupt hatching. Severe infestations may require dividing and replanting only clean rhizome sections.

subcategories.label: Bacterial leaf spot
subcategories.description: Brown or yellow spots on leaves during humid summer weather. Cosmetic only — rarely affects rhizome health. Improve air circulation by thinning crowded clumps. Severe: copper-based fungicide if needed.

plants.name: Pond Iris (Yellow Flag)
plants.guide: Yellow Flag shares the pond edge with the native Blue Flag — same strap-leaved, mud-anchored wetland habit, but bright yellow falls instead of violet. An introduced Eurasian species, and a vigorous colonizer: it spreads by both creeping rhizome and floating seed, which is exactly why its ribbed green seed pods are worth keeping an eye on around a pond. Handsome, tough, and happy to take more of the shoreline than you'd offer it — the one to keep in bounds.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Right now — bloom's finished and the seed pods have set. Observed late July 2026: fat, ribbed green capsules standing where the flowers were, in clusters at the pond edge. Left alone they'll ripen, split, and float seed off into the shallows to start new clumps, so snipping the spent stalks now — before the pods brown and open — is the way to keep Yellow Flag from taking over the pond. Peak bloom here runs mid-May into June.
plants.soilNotes: Lives in pond mud and shallow water (0–4 inches over the rhizome). The pond's accumulated organic sediment provides all nutrition needed. No amendment required. Tolerant of seasonal water-level fluctuation as long as the rhizome stays consistently moist.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun for best bloom. Tolerates light shade but flower count drops 30–50%. The pond location with open sky exposure is ideal. North-bank plantings get more sun (south-facing aspect into the pond); south-bank plantings get less.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy USDA Zone 4–9. Bulletproof and then some. A non-native (introduced Eurasian) species, entirely untroubled by North Georgia winters. Foliage dies back to the rhizome after first hard frost; new shoots emerge in April.

subcategories.label: Cut spent stalks before seed pods ripen
subcategories.peakWindow: Jun–Jul, before the green pods brown and split
subcategories.description: Snip spent flower stalks at the base as soon as bloom finishes, before the seed pods ripen and split. Yellow Flag seeds float and colonize fast, so on a pond this is the main thing standing between one tidy clump and a shoreline takeover. Removing the pods also redirects energy back into the rhizome.

subcategories.label: Cut back foliage in late fall
subcategories.peakWindow: After first hard frost flattens leaves
subcategories.description: Cut foliage to about 6 inches above the water surface after frost has killed back the leaves. Removing the dead foliage from the water reduces decomposition load on the pond and limits overwintering iris borer eggs (their preferred winter habitat is in old leaf debris).

propagate.description: Divide rhizomes every 3–5 years to prevent overcrowding. Lift the clump with a fork (or pull from the mud), wash off muck to expose the rhizome network, cut into sections each with a healthy fan of leaves and several inches of root. Replant immediately at the same depth as before — rhizome top barely covered, leaf bases above water. August–early September timing avoids stressing during peak summer heat and gives roots time to re-establish before winter.

fertilize.description: Light feeding only. Pond iris in established ponds rarely need fertilizer — the pond's organic load supplies plenty. If bloom is poor, slow-release aquatic fertilizer tablets (e.g. Pondtabbs) pushed into the mud around the rhizome in early spring help. Excessive fertilizer causes lush leaves at the expense of bloom and can drive pond algae blooms.

water.description: Not applicable — lives in the pond. No supplemental irrigation needed.

repot.description: Not applicable for pond-edge plantings. Container-grown specimens (rare for Blue Flag) would refresh aquatic potting mix every 2–3 years in early spring.

subcategories.label: Iris borer
subcategories.peakWindow: May 10–Jun 15 — larvae feed inside leaf bases
subcategories.description: The most serious iris pest. Adult moths lay eggs on dead foliage in fall; larvae hatch in spring and tunnel down through new leaves into the rhizome where they cause soft rot. Symptoms: water-soaked or 'bleeding' streaks on leaves; ragged chewed leaf edges; foul-smelling rhizomes. Control: remove and destroy ALL old foliage in late fall (eliminates overwintering eggs). If borers found in spring, squash them inside the leaf channel or remove the affected fan entirely. Iron-phosphate slug bait near the base in early spring can disrupt hatching. Severe infestations may require dividing and replanting only clean rhizome sections.

subcategories.label: Bacterial leaf spot
subcategories.description: Brown or yellow spots on leaves during humid summer weather. Cosmetic only — rarely affects rhizome health. Improve air circulation by thinning crowded clumps. Severe: copper-based fungicide if needed.

plants.name: Butterfly Weed
plants.guide: The butterfly weed on the property is a native milkweed that does well in these well-drained mountain soils. Bright orange flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) bloom June through August and are magnets for monarchs, swallowtails, and a wide range of native bees. Drought-tolerant once established — it resents wet feet and overwatering. Slow to emerge in spring; do not assume it has died and disturb the root. The deep taproot makes transplanting difficult, so site carefully.
plants.currentSeasonNote: May: plants should be actively growing and approaching bloom. CONFIRMED ISSUE at Church Mountain Road (May 2026): aphid infestation with severe distortion and curling of growing tips — small black dots visible on stems and leaves. Avoid systemic insecticides to protect monarch caterpillars and other pollinators. See Inspect section for treatment.
plants.soilNotes: Perfectly matched to Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet native soils — well-drained acidic sandy loam is ideal. Butterfly weed is native to dry rocky/sandy slopes and will rot in poorly drained heavy clay. On flat areas at Church Mountain Road where clay Bt subsoil impedes drainage, raised beds or high spots are strongly preferred. pH 6.0–7.0 is optimal; native soils at ~5.0 may benefit from a light lime amendment.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun — at least 6 hours of direct sun daily. South or west-facing open slopes are best. The species is native to dry open meadows and roadsides; it will decline in shade or with root competition from trees.
plants.frostSensitivity: Extremely cold-hardy (Zone 3). No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road. Very late to emerge in spring — do not disturb the crown before late April; emergence at ~2,959 ft elevation can be delayed until mid-May.

prune.description: Cut back last year's dead stems to ground level in late winter/early spring before new growth emerges. Do not cut back in fall — the dead stems provide winter habitat for native solitary bees. In early spring, check for bright orange-red shoots emerging at soil level before cutting.

subcategories.label: Seed
subcategories.peakWindow: Oct 1–20 — collect pods just as they split
subcategories.description: Collect seed pods in fall when they begin to split and before the silky floss carries seeds away. Cold stratification (30–60 days at 34–38°F in moist sand or paper towel) dramatically improves germination. Sow outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification, or stratify in the fridge and start indoors in March. Seedlings take 2–3 years to bloom.

subcategories.label: Root cuttings
subcategories.peakWindow: Mar — before growth begins
subcategories.description: Root cuttings are the most reliable vegetative method. Take 3–4 inch sections of root in late winter/early spring before emergence. Plant horizontally 1–2 inches deep. Roots are thick and brittle — work carefully. Plants grown from root cuttings typically bloom in 1–2 years.

fertilize.description: Do not fertilize. Butterfly weed evolved in poor, dry soils — excess nitrogen produces lush weak foliage that is more aphid-susceptible and fewer flowers. If plants are in good, well-drained soil, no supplemental fertilizer is needed or desirable.

water.description: Water weekly during the first year to establish the taproot. Once established (year 2+), butterfly weed is drought-tolerant and performs better with less water. Overwatering or waterlogged conditions will kill the plant. At Church Mountain Road, established plants should need no supplemental watering except during extended summer droughts.

repot.description: Not applicable — the deep taproot makes transplanting very difficult. Site carefully from the start.

subcategories.label: Aphid infestation
subcategories.peakWindow: May–Jun when new growth is most vulnerable
subcategories.description: CONFIRMED ISSUE at Church Mountain Road (May 2026): black aphid infestation with severe distortion and curling of growing tips. Small black dots on stems and leaves are the aphids or their frass. Do NOT use systemic insecticides — monarch caterpillars feed on these plants and would be killed. Management: (1) strong blast of water to knock aphids off; (2) insecticidal soap sprayed directly on affected areas; (3) tolerate moderate infestations — lady beetles and parasitic wasps often bring populations under control naturally within 2–3 weeks. Distorted growth will not recover; new growth after control should come in clean.

plants.name: Summer Cascade Wisteria
plants.guide: The Summer Cascade® wisteria on the property is a cultivar of Kentucky wisteria — a native North American species that does not share the invasive habits of Asian wisterias. Long cascading racemes of purple-dark lavender flowers bloom in June and again lightly through summer. Vigorous climber to 15–20 ft — needs a strong pergola, arbor, or trellis. Fragrant and deer-resistant. Unlike Asian wisterias, it blooms reliably without the 7–10 year wait.
plants.currentSeasonNote: May: vines are leafing out rapidly. Support training is critical now — tie new shoots to the structure in the direction you want them to grow. First bloom expected in June at ~2,959 ft elevation (a week or two later than valley plants). Do not prune now — wait until after the first bloom flush.
plants.soilNotes: Adaptable to Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils across a wide pH range (6.0–8.0). Prefers well-drained soil but tolerates occasional wet periods better than many vines. Avoid wet clay subsoil areas where root rot can occur. Mulch the root zone to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun — minimum 6 hours. South or west-facing fence or pergola is ideal for maximum bloom. Partial shade reduces flowering significantly. At Church Mountain Road, an open south-facing exposure will produce the best bloom.
plants.frostSensitivity: Very cold-hardy (Zone 4). No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road. As a native species, it is far better adapted to fluctuating early spring temperatures than Asian wisterias.

subcategories.label: Summer trim (after bloom)
subcategories.peakWindow: Late Jun–Jul — after first bloom flush
subcategories.description: After the main June bloom flush, cut back long whippy shoots to 5–6 leaves. This controls size, tidies the plant, and encourages secondary flower bud formation for later flushes. Do not cut back into the main framework at this time.

subcategories.label: Hard winter pruning
subcategories.peakWindow: Feb 1–20 before bud swell
subcategories.description: Late winter is the main structural pruning window. Cut back all lateral side shoots to 2–3 buds from the main framework. This concentrates energy into bloom rather than foliage and keeps the plant manageable. Also the time to train new shoots along the support structure.

propagate.description: Simple or serpentine layering in spring. Pin a flexible young shoot to the ground, wound the underside lightly, cover with soil. Roots form in 2–4 months; sever from parent the following spring. Most reliable vegetative method for home gardeners.

fertilize.description: Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers entirely — they promote lush foliage at the expense of flowers. If soil is very poor, a low-nitrogen fertilizer (e.g., 5-10-10) can be applied in late winter/early spring. Church Mountain Road native soils are generally adequate; most established wisterias need no fertilizing.

water.description: Water regularly during the first two years to establish a deep root system. Once established, wisteria is reasonably drought-tolerant. Consistent moisture during bloom development (May–June) supports a heavier flower display. Mulch the root zone to retain soil moisture.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape vine.

subcategories.label: Support structure integrity
subcategories.description: Check support structure in late winter before growth begins and again in fall. A mature wisteria exerts significant weight and leverage on trellises and pergolas. Ensure posts, anchors, and wires are secure. Wooden structures may need periodic reinforcing as the vine matures.

subcategories.label: Scale insects
subcategories.description: Look for small bumpy brown or white waxy scales on stems and older wood. Dormant oil spray in late winter/early spring (before bud break) is the most effective control. In summer, look for crawlers on new growth — insecticidal soap or neem oil when crawlers are active.

bloom.window: Late spring, then repeat flushes through summer
bloom.note: A summer-blooming native wisteria — reblooms after the first flush, unlike the aggressive Asian kinds.

plants.name: Elpis Clematis
plants.guide: The Elpis clematis here is a repeat-blooming large-flowered hybrid that puts up blooms from spring through fall. Grows 6–8 ft tall by 2–3 ft wide on a trellis or fence — ideal for vertical interest in mixed borders or against structures. Large flowers are a draw for bees and butterflies. Classic rule: 'feet in the shade, head in the sun' — shade the root zone with mulch or low plants while letting the top climb into full light.
plants.currentSeasonNote: May: expect early-season blooms developing now. Tie in new shoots gently to the support as they emerge — the stems are brittle and snap easily in wind. At ~2,959 ft elevation, first bloom may be a week later than valley plants.
plants.soilNotes: Requires well-drained soil amended with organic matter. Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils are adequate but benefit from generous compost amendment at planting. A slightly higher pH (6.5–7.0) than the native soil's 4.5–5.5 may be beneficial — a light lime application at planting is worthwhile. Avoid waterlogging — clematis wilt is more severe in poorly drained soils.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun to part shade. East-facing positions with morning sun and afternoon shade are ideal at Church Mountain Road — afternoon summer sun can scorch leaves and stress the plant. Keep roots shaded with 2–3 inches of mulch regardless of sun exposure.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4. No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road. May emerge a bit later than valley plants in spring — do not cut back too early in spring before checking for live buds.

prune.description: Elpis blooms on both old and new wood (Group 2). Can be left largely unpruned (just clean out dead stems) for early blooms on old wood, or cut back lightly (by 1/3 to 1/2) in early spring for a tidy plant with vigorous bloom. Remove all dead and damaged stems first, then decide how hard to cut back based on amount of live wood. Full renovation cuts in alternate years help maintain vigor.

propagate.peakWindow: Jun — internode cuttings when stems are semi-ripe
propagate.description: Take 3–4 inch internode cuttings (just below a leaf node) in late spring/early summer when stems are semi-ripe. Remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and root in perlite/peat mix under mist or in a plastic-covered propagator. Keep shaded and humid; rooting takes 4–6 weeks. May be protected by plant patents — check before propagating for distribution.

fertilize.peakWindow: Mar — before active growth; Jun — after first bloom flush
fertilize.description: Clematis are heavy feeders. Apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10) in early spring before growth begins, and a potassium-rich liquid fertilizer (e.g., tomato feed) after the first bloom flush to promote continued repeat blooming through summer. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds in late summer — they promote soft growth vulnerable to late-season disease.

water.description: Regular, consistent moisture is essential — clematis dislikes both drought and waterlogging. Mulch the root zone heavily (2–3 inches) to keep roots cool and moist. During hot dry spells in summer, deep watering 2–3 times per week may be needed. Drip irrigation or soaker hose at the base is ideal — keep foliage dry to reduce disease risk.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape vine.

subcategories.label: Clematis wilt
subcategories.peakWindow: May–Jun — most common in cool wet springs
subcategories.description: Sudden wilting and blackening of stems, often starting at a leaf node and moving rapidly up or down the stem. Cut affected stems back to healthy tissue immediately and discard (do not compost). Disinfect pruners between cuts. Plants almost always recover from below-ground buds — do not assume the plant is dead. Improve air circulation and avoid wetting foliage.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: White powdery coating on foliage during warm humid periods. More cosmetic than damaging at moderate levels. Improve air circulation. Potassium bicarbonate spray or neem oil controls light infestations. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizing which promotes susceptible soft growth.

plants.name: DreamCloud Reblooming Hydrangea
plants.guide: The DreamCloud® hydrangea on the property is part of the Endless Summer® series — a reblooming bigleaf that puts up large bright white mophead flowers on both old and new wood from early summer through fall. The reblooming habit is the key advantage over traditional bigleafs: even if old-wood buds are lost to a late frost or winter damage, new-wood buds form and bloom through the growing season. Pure white flowers hold their color well in partial shade.
plants.currentSeasonNote: May: check for emerging buds on old wood from last season. At ~2,959 ft elevation, first bloom will be later than valley plants — expect late June. If old-wood shoots were frost-damaged in a late freeze, do not panic: new-wood buds will develop and bloom through summer. Keep consistently watered as active growth accelerates in May.
plants.soilNotes: Prefers moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils at Church Mountain Road are acidic (4.5–5.5) — DreamCloud flowers white regardless of pH, unlike blue/pink bigleafs. Amend planting hole with generous compost. Avoid low spots with standing water or heavy clay subsoil that stays wet in winter.
plants.aspectPreference: Part sun to part shade. East-facing positions with morning sun and afternoon shade are ideal at Church Mountain Road — afternoon summer sun can scorch leaves and stress the plant. North-facing exposures also work well. Avoid full hot south or west exposure without supplemental water.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4 overall, but old-wood flower buds are vulnerable. At ~2,959 ft elevation, late frosts through mid-May can damage or kill buds formed on last year's growth — a real risk at Church Mountain Road. The reblooming genetics mean the plant will still flower on new wood, but the first bloom flush may be delayed. Protect with frost cloth during late spring freeze events if possible.

prune.peakWindow: Mar — after last hard freeze, before bud swell
prune.description: Prune conservatively in late winter — remove only clearly dead wood (brown, dried stems with no live buds). Do not cut back healthy stems as they carry the first bloom buds. After the first bloom flush (late June–July), lightly deadhead spent flowers and remove any weak or crossing stems. Full renovation cuts (to near ground level) can be done in late winter every 3–4 years to rejuvenate old plants, accepting one season of reduced bloom.

propagate.description: Take 4–5 inch tip cuttings from non-flowering stems in early summer. Remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and stick in a perlite/peat mix. Keep shaded and consistently moist. Rooting takes 4–6 weeks. May be protected by plant patents — check before propagating for distribution.

fertilize.description: Apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10 or azalea/rhododendron fertilizer) in early spring as growth begins. A second light application in May before bloom promotes strong flower development. Avoid fertilizing after July — late-season nitrogen promotes soft growth more susceptible to frost damage.

water.description: Bigleaf hydrangeas are among the most moisture-demanding landscape shrubs. Water deeply 2–3 times per week during hot dry stretches. Morning watering is preferred; avoid wetting foliage in the evening. Mulch 2–3 inches around the base to retain moisture and keep roots cool. At Church Mountain Road, the cooler climate and higher rainfall reduce stress compared to valley sites, but supplemental water is still needed during dry stretches.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape shrub.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces during warm, humid weather — common in late summer at Church Mountain Road. Primarily cosmetic. Improve air circulation around the plant. Potassium bicarbonate or neem oil spray for control if severe. Avoid overhead watering.

subcategories.label: Botrytis blight
subcategories.description: Gray fuzzy mold on flowers and buds during cool, damp weather — spring and fall are peak windows at this elevation. Remove and dispose of affected flower heads. Improve air circulation. Fungicide treatment rarely needed in landscape settings.

subcategories.label: Late frost bud damage
subcategories.peakWindow: Apr–early May — critical watch period at ~2,959 ft elevation
subcategories.description: Old-wood flower buds are vulnerable to late spring frosts. Check the 10-day forecast in April and early May. When a hard frost (<28°F) is predicted, cover with frost cloth or old bedsheets overnight. Even with bud loss, the reblooming genetics ensure bloom on new wood later in the season.

bloom.note: A reblooming bigleaf — flowers on both old and new wood, so a late frost won't cost the whole show.

plants.name: Pop Star Endless Summer Reblooming Hydrangea
plants.guide: The Pop Star hydrangea is a compact reblooming bigleaf that produces abundant lacey blue or pink mophead flowers on both old and new wood from early summer through fall. The reblooming habit is the defining trait — even if a late spring frost damages old-wood flower buds, new buds develop and bloom through the growing season. Flower color is soil pH dependent: acidic soils (4.5–5.5) yield blue; alkaline soils (above 7.0) yield pink. At Church Mountain Road's native pH, expect blue flowers without amendment. Low-maintenance, pollinator magnet, electric color in the landscape.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Late May at Church Mountain Road — the plant is leafed out and flower buds are swelling. First bloom should emerge in 2–3 weeks (early-to-mid June at ~2,959 ft elevation, about a week later than valley plants). Check for emerging buds on old wood from last season. If any shoots show frost damage from a late freeze, do not cut them back — new buds will develop and bloom on new wood through summer. Keep consistently watered as active growth accelerates.
plants.soilNotes: Thrives in Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils at Church Mountain Road. The native acidic pH (4.5–5.5) is ideal for blue flowers — no lime amendment needed. Bigleaf hydrangeas demand moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Amend the planting hole generously with compost at establishment. Avoid low spots with standing water or heavy clay subsoil that stays wet in winter — root rot is the enemy. On flat areas at the property where clay Bt argillic subsoil impedes drainage, use a raised or bermed bed position.
plants.aspectPreference: Part sun to part shade. East-facing positions with morning sun and afternoon shade are ideal at Church Mountain Road — afternoon summer sun can scorch leaves and stress the plant, reducing bloom. North-facing exposures work but may reduce flowering by 20–30%. Avoid hot south or west exposures without supplemental irrigation during July–September dry stretches. The property's east-facing mid-slope positions are textbook hydrangea habitat.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4 overall, but old-wood flower buds are vulnerable to late spring frosts. At ~2,959 ft elevation, the May 1–21 window is the critical frost-risk period for buds on last year's growth — a real concern at Church Mountain Road. The reblooming genetics mean the plant will still flower on new wood even if old-wood buds are lost, but the first bloom flush may be delayed or reduced. Protect with frost cloth during late spring freeze events if possible, or site in the thermal belt mid-slope position where frost risk is slightly lower than in hollows.

prune.peakWindow: Mar — after last hard freeze, before bud swell
prune.description: Prune conservatively in late winter (Feb–early Mar, before bud swell). Remove only clearly dead wood (brown, dried stems with no live buds). Do not cut back healthy stems as they carry the first bloom buds. At Church Mountain Road elevation, last hard freeze typically occurs around mid-April, so hold off major pruning until late February to March to avoid hitting it. After the first bloom flush (late June–July), lightly deadhead spent flower clusters and remove any weak or crossing stems. Full renovation cuts (to near ground level) can be done in late winter every 3–4 years to rejuvenate old plants, accepting one season of reduced bloom.

propagate.description: Take 4–5 inch tip cuttings from non-flowering stems in early summer (Jun–Jul). Remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and stick in a perlite/peat mix. Keep shaded and consistently moist. Rooting takes 4–6 weeks. The Pop Star cultivar may be protected by plant patents — check before propagating for distribution.

fertilize.description: Apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10 or azalea/rhododendron formulation) in early spring (Mar) as growth begins. A second lighter application in May before bloom promotes strong flower development. Avoid fertilizing after July — late-season nitrogen promotes soft growth more susceptible to frost damage. At Church Mountain Road's native soil pH, the azalea-specific formulations are ideal as they include micronutrients suited to acidic mountain soils.

water.description: Bigleaf hydrangeas are among the most moisture-demanding landscape shrubs. Water deeply 2–3 times per week during hot dry stretches (June–September). Morning watering is preferred; avoid wetting foliage in the evening. Mulch 2–3 inches around the base to retain moisture and keep roots cool. At Church Mountain Road, the cooler mountain climate and higher rainfall (estimated 62–68 in/yr at elevation) reduce stress compared to lowland sites, but supplemental water is still critical during the July–August dry window when afternoon thunderstorms can be sporadic.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape shrub.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces during warm humid weather — common in late summer at Church Mountain Road when RH climbs to 70–90%. Primarily cosmetic but worth managing. Improve air circulation around the plant. Potassium bicarbonate or neem oil spray for control if severe. Avoid overhead watering — wet foliage in evening promotes the disease.

subcategories.label: Botrytis blight
subcategories.description: Gray fuzzy mold on flowers and buds during cool, damp weather — spring (March–April) and fall (September–October) are peak windows at this elevation. Remove and dispose of affected flower heads. Improve air circulation. Fungicide treatment rarely needed in landscape settings.

subcategories.label: Late frost old-wood bud damage
subcategories.peakWindow: Apr–early May — critical watch period at ~2,959 ft elevation
subcategories.description: Old-wood flower buds are vulnerable to late spring frosts. At Church Mountain Road, check the 10-day forecast in April and early May. When a hard frost (<28°F) is predicted, consider covering with frost cloth or old bedsheets overnight. Even with old-wood bud loss, the reblooming genetics ensure strong bloom on new wood later in the season — this is the insurance policy built into the variety.

_phaseF.elevationFit: Excellent fit at 2,959 ft. Reblooming genetics mean late frost loss of old-wood buds won't prevent blooming. Cooler summer temps at elevation extend bloom season compared to lowland GA.
_phaseF.habitatHint: East-facing mid-slope with morning sun and afternoon shade. Avoid full south/west exposure without supplemental water.
